title: Strong Typhoon Champi Brings Wind and Rain Near Taiwan
summary:
Hundreds of flights in East Asia were cancelled on Friday as Typhoon Champi moved close to Taiwan's north-east coast. A typhoon is the name for a powerful tropical storm in this part of the Pacific Ocean, like a hurricane in the Atlantic.

Authorities said one person died after being swept away by waves. The storm also injured 171 people, and about 1,000 people left their homes to stay safe.

Earlier this week, Champi was the strongest storm on the planet so far this year. Its steady winds reached 185 miles per hour over the Philippine Sea, which is as strong as a Category 5 hurricane. It later weakened. On Friday afternoon, its wind gusts were about 119 miles per hour.

Weather agencies in Taiwan, Hong Kong and Japan expected the center of the storm, called the eye, to pass by without coming onto land in Taiwan. But a Taiwanese forecaster said this could not be completely ruled out if the storm stalls or wobbles.

Rain was expected to be heaviest on Saturday morning and to continue until Saturday evening. Officials asked people to stay away from coasts and mountains.

Work and classes were called off on Friday in nearly all of Taiwan's 22 counties and cities. People there call this a "typhoon holiday." Only Kinmen county, a group of islands west of the main island, kept schools and offices open.

In Japan's Okinawa area, nearly 8,400 homes lost power, and more than 160 flights were cancelled by four Japanese airlines. Heavy rain and wind also reached Batanes, Philippine islands south of Taiwan.

Champi is Japan's 30th typhoon this year, the most since 2013. Experts link the busy season to an unusually strong El Niño, a natural warming of the Pacific Ocean that happens every few years and can change weather around the world.
why_it_matters: A very active typhoon season shows how ocean patterns like El Niño can affect millions of people, and how warnings, closures and evacuations help keep communities safe.

background_read: Typhoons are giant spinning storms that form over warm ocean water in the western Pacific; in the Atlantic, the same kind of storm is called a hurricane.
Their strength is measured by wind speed, and the strongest ones match a Category 5 hurricane.
Places often hit by typhoons, such as Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines, close schools and offices and warn people to avoid coasts so they stay safe.
El Niño is a natural pattern in which Pacific Ocean water grows warmer than usual, which can feed stronger or more frequent storms in some regions.
